summary: The approach holds up. I re-derived the slice from the brief and got the same structure: FileIdExtd listing on a directory handle, links decided by reparse tag, one targeted probe, a paged struct-of-arrays store, and real-tree tests. The simpler alternatives are each ruled out by a measurement or a person's decision. FindFirstFile has no FileId, a node tree breaks the U-001 memory budget, and reading the MFT needs admin. Two of the three majors are too severe. M1 and M2 are rules held by convention whose failures happen only in code that does not exist yet (the tree slice, open-in-Explorer), or are already shown to the user (ProbeFailures). M1 and M2 should be minor. M3 is correctly major: it is an unmeasured, unrecorded source of wrong byte counts for the largest files on the drive, and the stale-listing effect it depends on has already been seen on this machine. All 11 minors are valid at minor. One gap was missed: the design drops the architecture's used-space comparison and does not record that it was deferred. The build measured about 49 GB of that gap on C:.

assessments.note: The design already states the rule in the 'ScanStore read API' contract. Links are not a trap: the key decision says links are 'recorded with 0 bytes and never entered'. So only HardlinkDuplicate entries carry raw bytes a reader could wrongly sum. Nothing in this slice reads bytes per entry. The window shows only Totals, and Totals apply the rule and are checked by the hardlink tests (true size charged once, SizeProbed on the charged record). ChargedSize/ChargedOnDisk would be new methods, not changes to existing ones, so they can go in before or with the tree slice without breaking any reader. That slice's own design and review read this contract note. The store-equals-Totals assertion is cheap and worth adding, but it does not justify a full lap for a slice whose delivered behaviour is correct.

The failure mode is limited and not silent. A probe that fails keeps the listing values, sets ProbeFailed and increments ProbeFailures. The Finished state shows a note when ProbeFailures > 0 (Main window component). The claim that SizeProbe builds the path of the first-seen record from the display path is a guess ('may be'). The first-repeat probe can open the current name, and that path already comes from the Scanner's (entryIndex, fullPath) stack built on the \\?\ root. Any name of a FileId returns the same FILE_STANDARD_INFO. The 3 probe failures on C: are unexplained. Files deleted between listing and probe during a 129 s scan of a live drive would explain them just as well. The real gap is narrow: the long-path case never runs the probe. Add a WOF file and a hardlink pair under the long, trailing-dot path. The Win32Path type and GetNativePath protect callers that do not exist yet.

Correctly major. The mechanism is not hypothetical here. The spike measured a directory entry 1 MiB stale on this PC. The build's sparse fixture had to be flushed because sizes lagged a writer that had not flushed (the listing and the handle both read 0). The files most likely to be held open (WSL/Docker .vhdx, VM disks, pagefile/swapfile) are also the largest. So the unrecorded error lands where the bytes are. The design recorded the narrower 'one name under the root' hardlink limit but not this one. One caveat on fix (a): a handle probe corrects stale EndOfFile and AllocationSize for an open, non-sparse file. It does not fix sparse allocation that has not been flushed yet, because the build measured the handle lagging there too.

Minor is right. The spike's tag tally on this PC shows no DFS, but the drive row offers Network drives, so the path can be reached. Both the dedup key with no volume part and the single choice of listing class rest on 'never leaves its volume', and the classifier's 'enter every other reparse directory' breaks that for tag 0x8000000A. Classifying the DFS tag as a link is the cheapest fix and keeps both assumptions true.

Minor is right, and the case is narrower than filed. Windows usually creates System Volume Information on a removable volume it mounts, so a truly empty FAT/exFAT root is rare. It can still be reached (for example, a freshly formatted stick with indexing off). The fix is to treat a single error code on the first RestartInfo call as an empty listing. Leaving the check to validate is right, since unit tests cannot build that volume.

Correct: with a sparse file or a plain file that has data, the fixture as described fails the sparse guard or the AllocationSize guard before the CloudOnly guard is reached. So deleting the CloudOnly check leaves the test green. The remedy works: compact with xpress4k, set OFFLINE, and assert the raw listing's shape before the scan.

Minor is right. One refinement to the fix: widening files to src/** will match Native/Kernel32.cs if it defines the FILE_ATTRIBUTE_REPARSE_POINT constant, so that file needs its own exception. The rule 'the scanner lists directories only through DirectoryReader' has the same narrow Scanning/** scope. A later 'rescan subtree' in Store or App using Directory.Enumerate* would get past it.
The design already guards v3's Assert.Skip*, which shows xUnit v3 is in scope. Explicit=true gets past every pattern listed. Minor.

The design has no fault ending. Pickers stay disabled by contract, so any exception from Scan (OOM past the 5M-entry budget, a parser bug) leaves the window unusable. Minor is right because it needs a bug or an extreme drive to happen.

Minor is right. The same per-folder granularity also means that one folder with hundreds of thousands of entries freezes the counters and delays Cancel until its listing finishes, even with no blocked I/O.
The build measured this directly ("C:\" reached the app as C:"), and the CLI is the route validate uses. The fix is trivial and a pure test can cover it. Minor.

Consistent with the symlink spike's measurement: CreateSymbolicLink succeeded in a token without SeCreateSymbolicLinkPrivilege, which means .NET already passes the unprivileged flag. The remedy is dead text, and the build confirms the fallback was never written. Q-001 instructed that remedy, so the disposition should report that Q-001's premise is contradicted by the spike. It should not rewrite Q-001's instruction inside the design on the reviewer's own authority. Q-001's rule that the test fails loudly and is never skipped is unaffected.

Does not conflict with Q-003, which allows the bootstrap. Pinning -Version 10.0.401 and checking the script's signature both fit inside that decision. Each worktree downloading the newest 10.0 band is real drift, because global.json's latestFeature accepts any 10.0.1xx or later. Minor.

Every item is on the build's deviation list, so later gates can see them in the open list. The design is still the document code-review and validate read, and in this engine a design that is not updated after the target moves has caused repeated laps. Minor is right because the deviations are recorded, not hidden.

missed.claim: The design leaves out the architecture's used-space comparison and does not say it is deferred. After a whole-drive scan, the user sees 'Finished: C:\' with an on-disk total about 49 GB below what the volume reports as used, and the only acknowledgement is a count of unreadable folders. Part of that gap is data no unprivileged listing can ever enumerate: the NTFS metafiles, where $MFT alone is roughly 4 GiB for about 4.1M records. Listing the unreadable folders therefore cannot explain it.
missed.evidence: Build left-open: 'The architecture's Scan Engine asks the volume for used space on a whole-drive scan, to show the coverage gap. This slice's design has no component for it. On C: this run found 685.8 GB on disk against about 735 GB used, with 599 unreadable folders.' The design's components, key_decisions and Main window 'Finished' description contain no used-space query and no deferral.
missed.fix: Either add one GetDiskFreeSpaceExW call on drive-root scans and show the unaccounted bytes in the Finished state, or record in key_decisions that the coverage gap is deferred to a named later slice and word Finished so it does not claim the whole drive. The registered read-denied-folders operation can measure how much of the gap the 599 folders hold.

payload.notes: The first reviewer's evidence is strong, with citations to docs and the build's own measurements, and none of the 14 findings is over-reach the design already answers. The skew is in the majors. Two of the three are rules held by convention, and the reviewer ranked each by what a future caller could do wrong (the tree slice's rollups, open-in-Explorer, delete), not by what fails in this slice. In both cases the delivered behaviour is correct or the failure is already shown to the user. The majors should be the findings about bytes this slice counts wrongly now, and only M3 is. The reviewer compared the design with the build's deviations (m11) but not with the architecture, so it missed a component the build itself flagged as absent. The frame holds: the only structurally different options are reading the MFT (needs admin) or System.IO enumeration (no FileId, AllocationSize or tag), and a spike or architecture rule excludes each.
